section.title: Disabled People (Employment)
section.p: Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if she will issue a Green Paper on employment for disabled people.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: I refer the hon. Member to the reply I gave to my hon. Friend, the Member for Exeter (Sir J. Hannam) on 26 January 1993, Official Report, column 659.
Mr. Illsley: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment under what circumstances it is her Department's policy to invoke prosecutions of employers under the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act 1944.

Mr. Michael Forsyth [holding answer 15 February 1993]: My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State believes that every effort should be made to educate and persuade employers to adopt positive employment policies towards disabled people and thereby comply with the Act.

Officials will therefore seek to resolve such matters by negotiation and advice wherever possible. Where this is unsuccessful or inappropriate, prosecution will be considered on the basis of the circumstances of the case, the strength of the evidence and the public policy interest.
Mr. Illsley: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment (1) under what circumstances an employer would be refused an application for bulk permits to employ people not registered disabled;
(2) how many applications for bulk permits to employ people not registered disabled have been refused in the last 15 years.

Mr. Michael Forsyth [holding answer 15 February 1993]: Responsibility for the subject of the question has been delegated to the Employment Service Agency under its chief executive. I have asked him to arrange for a reply to be given.

p.i: Letter from M. E. G. Fogden to Mr. Eric Illsley, dated 17 February 1993:
p.quote: As the Employment Service is an Executive Agency, the Secretary of State has asked me to write to you direct to respond to your Parliamentary Questions to her about bulk 246 permits. This is something which falls within the responsibilities delegated to me as Chief Executive of the Agency.

A bulk permit would be refused if my local Disability Employment Adviser considered that sufficient suitably qualified registered disabled people are likely to be available to fill the employers vacancies.

A bulk permit would also be refused where the employer fails to show they will take reasonable steps towards recruiting suitable registered disabled people. The permit is issued on the understanding the employer will notify vacancies to the Jobcentre and will consider sympathetically the engagement of any suitable registered disabled people.
I regret I am unable to say how many bulk permits have been refused in the last fifteen years as such information is not held centrally.

As decided by the Administration Committee of the House of Commons, Chief Executive replies to written Parliamentary Questions will now be published in the Official Report. I will also place a copy of this letter in the Library of the House.

section.p: Mr. Illsley: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment how many campaigns the Government have organised in the last 15 years to encourage disabled people to register their disabilities with her Department.

Mr. Michael Forsyth [holding answer 15 February 1993]: We have not run any specific campaign to encourage disabled people to register under the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act 1944. However disability employment advisers in local jobcentres provide disabled people with information about registering as disabled.

section.title: Transfer of Undertakings Regulations
section.p: Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment how the transfer of undertakings directive applies to takeovers by companies based in other EC countries of a British company.

Mr. Michael Forsyth [holding answer 16 February 1993]: The Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981 have the effect of 248 continuing certain statutory and contractual rights of employees when an undertaking is transferred from one employer to another. It is immaterial whether the employer in the United Kingdom is or becomes controlled by a company in another country within or outside the EC.

Mr. Aitken: My Department does not maintain records on the ownership of defence industrial capacity in other countries. However, on the information available to me, I understand that almost all of the warshipbuilding capacity in France and Italy is, effectively, state owned, while that in Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium is not.

Mr. Viggers: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will make a statement on current Independent European Programme Group-Western European Union arrangements for reciprocal purchasing in the field of warship hulls.

section.title: UNPROFOR II
section.p: Sir Nicholas Bonsor: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence which major unit has been warned off to relieve 1st Battalion the Cheshire Regiment as part of UNPROFOR II; when that unit last undertook an emergency tour, and where; from which other units reinforcements to that battalion will be drawn; when they last completed an emergency tour and where; whether soldiers from reinforcing units are trained to operate with Warrior armoured vehicles; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: 1 Prince of Wales Own Regiment from Osnabruck will replace I Cheshire Regiment, currently forming the basis of our battalion group in Bosnia, in May 1993. The Prince of Wales Own Regiment will be augmented by a platoon of Gordon Highlanders from Berlin; a platoon of the Queen's Lancashire Regiment from Berlin; and a platoon of 1 Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders from Minden.

Other units of the present battalion group will be replaced by a squadron of Light Dragoons from Hohne —to replace the squadron from 9/12 Lancers—and elements of 21 Engineer Regiment from Nienburg—to replace elements of 35 Engineer Regiment. Soldiers from units deploying are trained to work with Warrior armoured vehicles.

section.title: HMS Calpe
section.p: 87. Sir Nicholas Bonsor: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence what is the current role, annual cost and strength of the headquarters unit at HMS Calpe, Gibraltar; when he intends to close it; how and by whom its wartime task will be fulfilled henceforth; what role HMS Calpe played in the seatrain during Operation Granby; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: The current rule of HMS Calpe is to provide Royal Naval Reserve personnel to undertake naval control of shipping duties. The unit also provides additional operational support to the Commander British Forces Gibraltar including some augmentation to the manning of the maritime headquarters in periods of tension and war. The annual cost of the unit is £180,000. The strength is 21 officers, 56 ratings and three civilians. HMS Calpe will close by 31 March 1993. In future, the naval control of shipping tasks will be undertaken by staff deployed from the United Kingdom should the need arise. Tasks previously undertaken by RNR personnel serving in the maritime headquarters will now be undertaken by service personnel using modern visual aids and computers. HMS Calpe was not involved in the seatrain during Operation Granby.

Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will make it his policy for the Benefits Agency to establish a dedicated advice line for carers.
Mr. Scott: Operational matters are a matter for Mr. Michael Bichard, the chief executive of the Benefits Agency. He will write to the hon. Member and a copy will be placed in the Library.

p.i: Letter from Michael Bichard to Mr. Dafydd Wigley, dated 16 February 1993:
p.quote: As Chief Executive of the Benefits Agency, it is my responsibility to answer questions about relevant operational 252 matters. I am therefore replying to your recent Parliamentary Question to the Secretary of State for Social Security asking if the Agency will establish a dedicated advice line for carers.

The Agency is committed to providing both an efficient and effective service accessible to all our customers. To this end, specific consideration has been given to people with disabilities and those who care for them, and a number of initiatives have been set up.

With the success of the general Freeline service a number of similar services were introduced including the Benefit Enquiry Line (BEL). This provides advice and information to people with disabilities as well as to the people who care for them. It is also able to assist with the completion of claim forms over the telephone. At present, forms can be completed for visually impaired customers in braille or large print. However, as a development of the BEL, a full form completion service covering the full range of benefits for people with disabilities and their carers will be introduced in April this year. The benefits covered will include Disability Living Allowance, Disability Working Allowance, Attendance Allowance, Severe Disablement Allowance and Invalid Care Allowance.
With carers being catered for by the Benefit Enquiry Line the Agency does not have any plans, at this stage, to establish a further advice line.
I hope you find this reply helpful. A copy will appear in the Official Report. A copy will also be placed in the Library.

p.i: Letter from Michael Bichard to Ms. Mildred Gordon, dated 15 February 1993:
p.quote: As Chief Executive of the Benefits Agency it is my responsibility to answer questions about relevant operational matters. I am therefore replying to your recent parliamentary question to the Secretary of State for Social Security about the time taken to respond to correspondence by the Benefits Agency in Leeds.

You ask what percentage of letters in the past twelve month period have been cleared within 20 working days and what percentage took six months or over to reply. The information for 1992 is as follows:

tr.td: Total replies to Members from Chief Executive:
of which, Replied within 20 working days

p.quote: I very much regret that the Benefits Agency has not recently been meeting its target for responding to Members' letters and that some very long delays have occurred. As I explained in my letter to you of 27 January on an individual case you had raised, the delays are due to the backlog of correspondence that has built up in the Disability Living Allowance Unit following the greater than expected workload faced by the Unit in the early months of the DLA scheme.

The delay in replying to Members' letters about DLA does not, of course, mean that action is not proceeding on a customer's claim. In fact in most cases where there is a long outstanding reply the claim will have been resolved much earlier. You will recall that in the case discussed in my letter of 27 January, full benefit entitlement was paid in September 1992. I understand this followed contact you had with the special Hotline telephone enquiry service for Members I have set up at the DLA Unit. But clearly you should have had a reply to your letter from me much sooner than you did and apologise for this.

A recovery plan for clearing the backlog of correspondence at the DLA Unit is now in operation with a view to substantially reducing the number of letters awaiting reply by the end of this month. Once the backlog is cleared it will be our aim to respond to all future correspondence on DLA, within the Agency's target of twenty working days, as is already the case for correspondence about other subjects.
I hope you find this reply helpful. A copy will appear in the Official Report and a copy will also be placed in the Library.

section.title: Regional Assistance
section.p: 17. Mr. O'Hara: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what was the number of regional assistance grants paid to businesses in Knowsley in each of the past three years.

Mr. Sainsbury: In the three years to the end of March 1992 my Department supported in the Knowsley area 41 projects with regional selective assistance; 69 projects with regional development grants—the revised scheme — and 54 projects with regional enterprise grants.
I will publish a more detailed breakdown of these grants in the Official Report.
In addition, I am announcing this afternoon a grant of £799,000 to Kodak to extend its Acornfield road factory on the Knowsley industrial park.

td.i: Number of projects in the local authority district of Knowsley supported by RSA, RDG, or REG 1989–90 to 1991–92

section.title: Pâté de Foie Gras
section.p: 18. Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make it his policy to ban the import of pâté de foie gras into the United Kingdom; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Needham: No.

section.title: Free Flight Offers
section.p: 19. Mr. Donohoe: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what further steps he has taken to regulate free flight offers which accompany the sale of goods or services.
24. Mr. Jim Cunningham: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what further steps he has taken to regulate free flight offers which accompany the sale of goods or services.
Mr. Leigh: I have no evidence that such offers are other than bona fide sales promotions and have no plans for specific regulation of them.

section.title: Deregulation
section.p: 20. Mr. Sproat: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how he proposes to monitor deregulation throughout Whitehall.

Mr. Neil Hamilton: Progress under the deregulation initiative in all regulatory departments is co-ordinated and monitored by the central deregulation unit in my Department. As the Minister with particular responsibility, for the initiative, I take an active lead in liaising with deregulation Ministers in other Departments and monitoring their activities.

section.title: Railway Rolling Stock
section.p: 21. Mr. Bayley: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what help his Department is giving British railway rolling stock manufacturing.

Mr. Sainsbury: My Department supports the UK railway equipment manufacturers under its schemes of regional selective assistance, innovation and export promotion. My right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer announced in the autumn statement additional measures to release £150 million for rolling stock orders by British Rail. In addition, he announced the Government's continuing commitment to the Jubilee line extension.

section.title: Coal Mines (Wales)
section.p: 22. Mr. Wigley: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will state, on the basis of the latest information available to him, what are the prospects for each of the four remaining coal mines in Wales; and what discussions he has had with the NCB of plans for the sinking of new mines in Wales.
Mr. Eggar: Betws and Taff Merthyr are the subject of a consultation process currently being conducted by British Coal. Point of Ayr is being considered in the context of the coal review.
We have had no discussions with British Coal about opening new mines in Wales.

section.title: Japanese-owned Plants
section.p: 23. Mr. Fabricant: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what assessment he has made of the benefits to United Kingdom industry of experience of working practices in Japanese-owned plants in the United Kingdom.

Mr. Sainsbury: My Department keeps a watching brief on all relevant aspects of inward investment. I am particularly encouraged by the experience of Japanese investors in adapting their own working practices to UK circumstances. I have also noted that a number of UK companies have learnt from these practices.

section.title: Ireland (Market Development Fund)
section.p: 25. Mr. Trimble: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what response he has received from the European Commission with regard to his representations on the Republic of Ireland's market development fund.

Mr. Needham: As a result of representations made to the European Commission a number of important changes were made to the initial proposal so as to minimise the potential impact on United Kingdom businesses. The scheme is confined to companies employing fewer than 250 people and whose turnover does not exceed 20 mecu. Companies which are more than one quarter owned by one or more larger companies are ineligible. The aid is limited for a maximum of six months and will end in March 1993. The scheme can also be suspended if the average rate of sterling against the Irish pound closes below parity within any working week. I understand the Commission has ruled out any extension.

section.title: Pit Closures
section.p: 26. Mr. Corbyn: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on his latest proposals regarding coal mine closures.

Mr. Heseltine: We are engaged in a wide-ranging review of the prospects for 21 of the pits proposed for closure by British Coal, in the context of the Government's energy policy. We will shortly be publishing a White Paper setting out the results of that review, which will then be debated by the House.

section.title: Steel Exports (USA)
section.p: 27. Mrs. Helen Jackson: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what steps he is taking to protect steel exports to the United States of America.

Mr. Heseltine: I raised this subject with Barbara Franklin, the then United States Secretary of Commerce, by letter on 11 December. I have also written to her successor, Ron Brown, urging him to focus on these matters at the earliest opportunity.

The issue was raised at the Foreign Affairs Council on 2 February, when the United Kingdom joined other member states in condemning the United States actions as unacceptable. As a result the Community has requested formal consultations with the United States in accordance with the GATT subsidies code.
In addition, the EC fully supported Brazil in its denunciation of the United States decisions at the GATT Council on 9 February.

section.title: Timeshare Companies
section.p: 28. Dr. Wright: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what further steps he is taking to protect consumers against disreputable timeshare companies.
Mr. Leigh: The EC Commission has submitted a draft directive on timeshare to the Council of Ministers. The United Kingdom is seeking to secure the early adoption of this directive.

section.title: Gas (Exempt Supplies) Act 1993
section.p: 29. Mr. Duncan: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on the entry into force of the Gas (Exempt Supplies) Act 1993.

Mr. Eggar: We have made it clear that the Gas (Exempt Supplies) Act 1993 will not come into force until the Health and Safety Commission has had sufficient time to put appropriate safety arrangements in place. We therefore plan to bring the Act into force once revisions to the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1984 are in place, probably early in 1994.

section.title: One-stop Shops
section.p: 30. Mr. Lidington: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what progress his Department is making towards setting up one-stop shops.

Mr. Heseltine: A total of 57 partnerships have submitted bids for funding pilot one-stop shops. Many of these bids cover wide geographical areas and make proposals for establishing one-stop shops in more than one local area. This is an excellent response. I intend to announce the winning bids by the end of March.

section.title: Steel Exports (USA)
section.p: 31. Mr. Gapes: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what representations have been made by Her Majesty's Government in relation to penal tariffs on the importation of steel into the United States of America.

Mr. Heseltine: I raised this with Barbara Franklin, the then United States Secretary of Commerce, by letter on 11 December. I have also written to her successor, Ron Brown, urging him to focus on these matters at the earliest opportunity.

section.title: Post Office
section.p: 32. Mr. Gordon Prentice: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will estimate the current value of the assets of the Post Office.
Mr. Leigh: The value of the Post Office's net assets at 27 September 1992, as reported in the 1992–93 half-year results, was £2,205 million.

Ms Estelle Morris: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how many Crown post offices have been closed in each of the last five years; and what number of Crown post offices there are expected to be by the end of 1993.

Mr. Leigh [holding answer 15 February 1993]: The figures requested are as follows:
Year Number of Crown office closures
1987–88 4
1988–89 6
1989–90 154
1990–91 172
1991–92 148
Up to 31 January 1993 57
Total 541

These outlets have been replaced by 529 new agency-operated outlets which offer the full range of transactions and in many cases extended hours of opening. The Post Office will continue to review the opportunities for conversion of Crown offices to agency status throughout 1993.
Ms Estelle Morris: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how many (a) franchised post offices and (b) non-franchised sub-post offices there are expected to be by the end of 1993.

Mr. Leigh [holding answer 15 February 1993]: There are at present 53 franchise post offices and 18,974 sub-post offices in operation. The Post Office will review opportunities for further franchise offices as they arise throughout 1993 and some modest increase can be expected. The number of sub-post offices is expected to be broadly similar at the end of 1993, although closures occur from time to time as a result of local circumstances. The Government are committed to the maintenance of a nationwide network of post offices.
Ms Estelle Morris: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how many (a) crown post offices and (b) sub-post offices have become franchised sub-post offices in each of the last five years.

Mr. Leigh [holding answer 15 February 1993]: Since 1990 42 Crown offices have been converted to franchise status operating in major retail outlets such as supermarkets and newsagents. Five existing sub-post offices have been upgraded to franchise status. There have also been six openings of franchise offices in entirely new locations. No franchise offices were opened before 1990.

section.title: Motor Industry (Energy Strategy)
section.p: 33. Mr. Simon Coombs: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what plans he has to meet motor manufacturers to discuss the implications for the motor industry of his revised energy strategy.
Mr. Sainsbury: None.

section.title: Coal Industry
section.p: 34. Mr. Mullin: To ask the President of the Board of Trade when he expects to announce his plans for the future of the coal industry; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Heseltine: I hope to set out the Government's plans for the future of the coal industry in a White Paper to be published later this month.

Mr. Mullin: To ask the President of the Board of Trade whether the cost of continued pumping at pits in the Durham coalfield was taken into account (a) before the announcement of the proposed closures and (b) in the recent review of their viability.

Mr. Eggar [holding answer 15 February 1993]: The factors which British Coal considered before making its announcement of proposed pit closures on 13 October are a matter for the corporation. The studies by John T. Boyd Company of pits proposed for closure have taken account of the costs of pumping at those pits.

section.title: United States of America
section.p: 35. Mr. Gallie: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on trade with the United States of America.

Mr. Heseltine: The United States is our largest trading partner outside Europe and our trading relationship is therefore of the greatest significance. I have already conveyed to my counterparts in the new Administration the importance I attach to finding constructive solutions to the current EC-US bilateral issues, particularly in the steel and vehicles sector, and in bringing the Uruguay round to a successful conclusion. The position adopted by the EC Commission in its talks last week with the United States Administration on these matters has our full support.

The reviving United States economy provides considerable opportunities for British companies in the United States. I hope shortly to announce a major new campaign to encourage our exporters to seize these opportunities.

section.title: Postage Stamps (Royal Emblems)
section.p: 36. Ms. Hoey: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what consideration he has given to the future use of royal emblems on postage stamps in connection with his proposals to privatise the Post Office.
Mr. Leigh: The review of Post Office organisation and structure is not yet complete. No decision has been taken to privatise the Post Office. Full consideration is being given to all relevant issues.

section.title: Arms Conversion
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make it his policy to consult the Secretary of the National Steering Committee of Nuclear Free Zone Local Authorities about arms conversion.
Mr. Sainsbury: No.

section.title: Laboratories (Expenditure)
section.p: Mr. Cousins: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what is the expenditure of (a) the Warren Spring Laboratory, (b) the National Engineering Laboratory, 260 (c) the National Physical Laboratory and (d) the Laboratory of the Government Chemist in each year since 1989; what is the projected expenditure for the next three years; and how much income was generated from (i) Government sources outside his Department and (ii) non-Government sources since 1989.

Mr. Leigh: Responsibility for the subject of the question has been delegated to the chief executives of the four agencies concerned. I have therefore asked Dr. Richard Worswick, Laboratory of Government Chemist; Mr. William Edgar, National Engineering Laboratory; Dr. Peter Clapham, National Physical Laboratory; and Dr. Doug Cormack, Warren Spring Laboratory, to arrange for replies to be given.

I have been asked to reply in respect of the Agency for which I am responsible, the National Physical Laboratory.
The historic information requested is as follows:

It is expected to finance current expenditure (including capital charges) from income from payments by customers, principally Government Departments (including the Department of Trade and Industry), for work commissioned. LGC undertakes work for customers on a full economic cost basis.
Against this background, the details you requested about LGC's Vote Expenditure and Receipts are as follows:

section.p: I hope this information is helpful.

section.title: Coal Imports
section.p: Sir David Steel: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what estimates he has made of the change in the price of imported coal in 1992 due to currency fluctuations.

Mr. Eggar: Based on figures of spot purchases of coal delivered to Europe, published by the International Coal Report, the sterling price of imported coal declined from 93p per gigajoule in January 1992 to 74p per GJ in September, mainly due to a decline in the dollar price of imported coal. The price increased to 92p per GJ in December due to the exchange rate changes.

section.title: Manufactures
section.p: Mr. Spearing: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will list the manufactured products which have ceased to be manufactured in the United Kingdom since 1980.
Mr. Sainsbury: There are a number of sources of information on manufacturing products, but none is sufficiently comprehensive to allow for an accurate answer.

section.title: KissLine
section.p: Mr. Dickens: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what steps are being taken in connection with the KissLine telephone service; and what steps are being taken to prevent such services from being advertised in children's comics.

Mr. Leigh: The Independent Committee for the Supervision of Standards of Telephone Information Services sets and reviews standards relating to premium rate telephone services through the ICSTIS code of practice. ICSTIS recognises that children are a vulnerable audience for premium rate services and the code of practice contains a number of measures which help to protect children and their parents. Children's services must not, for example, include references to practices that a reasonable parent would not wish his or her child to hear or learn about in this way.

ICSTIS has considered the children's service entitled "Kissing: All the Secrets" and has decided that the content of the service was so mild that the appearance of an advertisement for it in a children's comic did not breach the ICSTIS code of practice.

section.title: Bank of Credit and Commerce International
section.p: Mr. Vaz: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what representations he has received concerning the lack of staff representation on the interim creditor committee of BCCI.
Mr. Neil Hamilton: Such representations have been received from the hon. Member for Leicester, East and from members of the BCCI campaign committee.

section.title: Insolvency Act
section.p:
Mr. Dowd: To ask the President of the Board of Trade how many individual voluntary arrangements under part VIII of the Insolvency Act 1986 have been notified to his Department in each of the last three years for which records are available; what is the total value of debt
263 written off in this fashion over this period; how many businesses have thereby been thus enabled to continue trading; and how many creditors have suffered irrecoverable losses as a result of the operation of this part of the Act.

Mr. Neil Hamilton: The number of individual voluntary arrangements in each year are published on my Department's behalf in "Business Briefing" by the Association of British Chambers of Commerce, copies of which are available in the Library. The further information sought by the hon. Member is not maintained and could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: European Structural Funds
section.p: Mr. Coe: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he considers that Cornwall should be eligible for grants from the European structural funds.

Mr. Sainsbury: Yes. The Government believe that Northern Ireland, the highlands and islands, Merseyside, Devon and Cornwall, rural Wales and South Yorkshire should be eligible for grants under objective 1 of these funds.

section.title: Industrial Strategy
section.p: Mr. Jim Marshall: To ask the President of the Board of Trade what is the Government's industrial strategy; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Heseltine: I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave to my hon. Friend the Member for Rugby and Kenilworth (Mr. Pawsey) on 16 November 1992, Official Report, column 71, and the answer given by my right hon. Friend the Minister for Industry to my hon. Friend the Member for Macclesfield (Mr. Winterton) on 27 January 1993, Official Report, column 735.

section.title: Dounreay
section.p: Mr. Dalyell: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on the future of Dounreay.

Mr. Eggar: The prototype fast reactor at Dounreay is due to cease operation on 31 March 1994, after which decommissioning operations will commence. Other decomissioning and radioactive waste management operations already under way will continue for some time to come. Dounreay is also the base of the Atomic Energy Authority's fuel services business. Future commercial activities there are a matter for the AEA.

section.title: Hospital Radio
section.p: Mr. Illsley: To ask the President of the Board of Trade (1) what discussions have taken place between his Department and the National Association of Hospital Broadcasting Organisations regarding the allocation of an FM frequency for hospital broadcasting services;
(2) whether the use of a freely radiating FM frequency will be made available to hospital broadcasting services.
Mr. Leigh [holding answer 15 February 1993]: I refer the hon. Gentleman to the answer that I gave on 9 February 1993, Official Report, column 569.

section.title: Value Added Tax
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will publish a table of information showing for regions of the United Kingdom, with Greater London shown as a separate region, the number of VAT registrations and de-registrations for each year since 1979.

Mr. Leigh [holding answer 15 February 1993]: Regional estimates of VAT registratio:ns and deregistrations, for the years 1980 to 1991, were published in CSO bulletin (5/93) on 15 January 1993, a copy of which is available in the Library.

section.title: International Atomic Energy Authority
section.p: Mr. Dalyell: To ask the President of the Board of Trade if he will make a statement on the IAEA meeting in Oslo from 1 to 5 February on dumping in the Kara and Barents seas.
Mr. Curry: I have been asked to reply.

The meeting was held under the joint auspices of the International Atomic Energy Authority, the Norwegian Radiation Protection Authority and the Federal Hydrometeorological Committee of Russia. Officials from the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food and from the Ministry of Defence attended.

The meeting launched "The International Arctic Seas Assessment Project (IASAP) 1993–95", a scientific programme designed to assess the implications for human health and the environment of radioactive wastes dumped in the Kara and Barents seas by the former Soviet Union and to consider any necessary remedial action. I welcome the co-operation being offered by the Russian authorities and look forward to seeing the results of this investigation.

section.title: Grant-maintained Schools
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) which company won the contract for printing the brochure, "Grant-maintained Schools-Questions Staff Ask"; if the contract was open to competitive tender; and what was the total cost of production and distribution;

(2) which company won the contract for printing the brochure, "Grant-maintained Schools-Questions Parents Ask"; if the contract was open to competitive tender; and what was the total cost of production and distribution;

(3) which company won the contract for printing the brochure, "How to become a Grant-maintained School"; for school governors; if the contract was open to competitive tender; and what was the cost of production and distribution.

Sir Wyn Roberts: These booklets were produced for the Welsh Office by the Central Office of Information and details relating to their production are a matter for the chief executive of COI. The production and distribution cost of each booklet cannot be separately identified as all three were produced together. The cost of producing and distributing all booklets was £23,900.

section.title: Contracting Out
section.p: Mr. McAllion: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will provide figures for the reduction in numbers of posts as a result of contracting out since 1979 in his Department and agencies for which he has responsibility.
Mr. David Hunt: Information in the form requested is not readily available and could be compiled only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act
section.p: Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what action is currently undertaken by his Department to ensure that local authorities fulfil obligations outlined in section 2 of the Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: We expect local authorities to be well aware of their statutory duties under section 2(1) of the 1970 Act, to provide a range of services for disabled people, where they accept that there is an assessed need. Each case is assessed on its own merits and the decision as to the kind of assistance to be provided is for the local authority to make, being best placed to judge an individual's needs. The Department receives annual returns and, as appropriate, follows up specific cases referred to the Department, where it is alleged that a local authority is in breach of its statutory duties.

section.title: Mental Illness
section.p: Mr. Barry Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) what new money and transitional funding he has allocated to each county in Wales in respect of the all-Wales mental illness strategy 1993–94; and if he will make a statement;
(2) if he will allocate extra funding to the all-Wales mental illness strategy; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: The allocation has been announced of an extra £1·2 million for 1993–94, in addition to what is required to maintain existing projects. The distribution of the allocation has yet to be decided. Discussions are continuing about the amount and duration of transitional funding needed to develop new services within each county.

section.title: Energy Conservation
section.p: Mr. Barry Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what initiatives he will take to boost energy conservation in Wales.

Mr. David Hunt: I have already taken several initiatives to encourage the efficient use of energy. In December 1991 I launched the "Energy Plan for Wales for the 1990s", which outlines our approach to energy conservation. A copy has been placed in the Library of the House. At the same time I wrote to all local authorities stressing the importance of energy conservation.

Very recently I have supplemented this initiative by joining the corporate commitment campaign started by my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for the Environment. This campaign is aimed at top management of both the commercial and public sectors. I myself signed the commitment on behalf of the Welsh Office last December. Details of this campaign have also been placed in the Library of the House.
My officals are at present very active in promulgating this message throughout Wales.

section.title: Community Care
section.p: Mr. Barry Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will make available extra funding for community care in 1993–94; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: I refer the hon. Gentleman to my announcement of 2 October that £35·9 million will be made available to local authorities in 1993–94 to meet the cost of their new responsibilities for community care. This includes the Department of Social Security transfer of £27·5 million, with a further £8·4 million for additional costs.

section.title: Schools and Colleges
section.p: Mr. Ron Davies: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many (a) infant schools, (b) primary schools, (c) secondary schools and (d) colleges of further education there were in Wales in each year since 1979; and how many places were offered by each category.

Mr. David Hunt: The number of infant, primary and secondary schools and colleges of further education in Wales in each year since 1979 is shown in the following table together with the total number of full and part-time pupils in schools and the number of enrolments in further education colleges. Information on the number of places offered by each category is not collected centrally.

tr.td: 2 At November each year. All colleges offering further education courses each year (both further education and higher education

section.p: colleges) are included in the table. The total number of further education enrolments is also shown irrespective of whether the course was run at a further education or higher education establishment.

section.title: Class Sizes
section.p: Mr. Ron Davies: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what was the average class size of (a) primary schools, (b) secondary schools, (c) sixth form colleges, (d) colleges of further education, (e) colleges of higher education and (f) infant schools in each year since 1979.

Mr. David Hunt: The average class size in primary and secondary schools and further and higher education courses in Wales since 1979 is shown in the following table. Figures are not available for further and higher education courses before 1982–83 and for secondary schools before 1986–87. Information on the average class size of infant schools and sixth form colleges is not collected separately. Information for the colleges of the University of Wales is not available.
