These data, relating to the numbers of classes by size, are given in the Secondary Education section of 'Statistics of Education in Wales: Schools', copies of which are available in the Library.

2 Average class sizes for Wales are calculated on a further education or higher education basis and the figures do include a small number of further education courses run at higher education establishments and higher education courses at further education establishments.
3 Changes in methodology, introduced in 1988–89, may affect comparisons of indicators between 1987–88 and 1988–89.

section.title: Waiting List Initiative
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what guidelines he has given to purchasers and providers of health care concerning the use of marginal cost pricing for waiting list initiative expenditure; in what circumstances purchaser-provider arrangements for operations can be based on marginal cost pricing; and if she will make a statement.

Mr. Gwilym Jones: Negotiations between purchasers and providers, whether in respect of mainstream business, or specific initiatives such as that on waiting times, take place within the well-established ground rules for NHS contracting.

section.title: Office Furniture
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what plans he has to order office furniture before 31 March; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. David Hunt: Orders to the value of approximatey £600 are waiting to be placed. Futher purchases may be made as required.

section.title: Halon Bank
section.p: Mr. Couchman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what proposals he has for establishing a United Kingdom halon bank.

Mr. Maclean: The Government do not plan to establish a Government-run United Kingdom halon bank. However, following discussions between Government halon users and the fire industry, I am pleased to announce the establishment of the project phase of the Halon Users' National Consortium (HUNC). HUNC is being set up by halon users and the fire industry with the aim of managing the United Kingdom installed bank of halons. It will act as a clearing house putting those who need to continue using halons in contact with those who do not. Unlike halon bank management proposals elsewhere in the world, HUNC will be a non-profit making organisation. It will be funded by members' subscriptions rather than from a levy on sales.

As its contribution to HUNC, my Department is funding publicity which is being issued to UK halon users this week. The set up costs for HUNC are being met by halon users and the fire industry. This is an excellent example of Government and industry co-operation.

section.title: Office of Water Services
section.p: Mr. French: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) what plans he has to increase the transparency of Ofwat;
(2) what plans he has to review the powers and accountability of Ofwat;
(3) what representations he has received concerning the powers and accountability of Ofwat; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Maclean: The Director General of Water Services already operates an open regulatory regime, for example by consulting widely on issues such as future charging policy. The responses to these public consultations inform his decisions, which are published in press releases. Information notes are also available which explain Ofwat policy.

The powers of the Director General were reviewed in preparation for the Competition and Service (Utilities) Act 1992, which enhanced his powers in certain respects, for example in the resolution of disputes.

The Director General reports each year to the Secretary of State on the discharge of his duties. The Secretary of State lays a copy of the report before Parliament, and Select Committees may call the Director General to give evidence. Whilst my Department occasionally receives representations from consumers about the powers and accountability of the Director General, I have no current plans to review them further.

section.title: Pay-when-paid Policy
section.p:
Mr. Ancram: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will provide details of the pay-when-paid policy of the Property Services Agency and of its
269 purpose and origins; and if he will make a statement on the application to this policy of the Government's requiring Departments to pay their private contractors as quickly as possible.

Mr. Redwood: New payment arrangements are being implemented by the PSA building management businesses, where they are acting as agents for the Ministry of Defence for payment purposes under MOD property management contracts, such that subcontractors are paid no later than seven days following receipt of payment from the client, MOD. There is an existing obligation on the MOD to pay promptly and this together with the new payment arrangements being adopted by the PSAS will ensure that subcontractors should be paid within 30 days from validation.

The development of the appropriate systems and procedural changes is underway so that by 1 April 1993 the five BM businesses are operating on this new basis. As these arrangements are introduced, I am demanding better performance from PSA in reducing delays in payments to contractors by getting invoices to MOD more promptly.

These arrangements create a contractual commitment on the managing contractor to make payment to subcontractors whose invoices have been accepted for payment by MOD and should be distinguished from other forms of "pay-when-paid" for capital works contracts whereby main contractors may withhold payments to subcontractors. This latter practice is inconsistent with the Government's prompt payment policy.

While the building management businesses are still in Government ownership, and they retain the obligations of the Government's prompt payment policy in their own right, a safety net will be in place so that PSA can ensure prompt payment to its contractors even where MOD has not paid PSA.

section.title: Landfill
section.p: Mr. Pike: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment when his Department intends to implement section 61 of the Environmental Protection Act 1990.
Mr. Maclean: My right hon. and learned Friend is still considering the appropriate time to implement section 61 of the Environmental Protection Act 1990.

section.title: Lambeth Council
section.p: Mr. Fraser: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what estimates he has made of that part of Lambeth's current notional expenditure which consists of (a) interest charges and (b) debt write-off.

Mr. Robin Squire: The relevant notional amount specified for Lambeth in "The Limitation of Council Tax and Precepts (Relevant Notional Amounts) Report (England) 1993–94" reflects the authority's own estimate of the amounts of interest charges and debt write-off which it made when setting its 1992–93 budget and community charges.
Mr. Fraser: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment how much Lambeth council is currently permitted to borrow excluding capital projects.

Mr. Robin Squire: The limit on an authority's borrowing is its aggregate credit limit (ACL), or any lower 270 limit the authority itself may have set. The ACL is determined by a formula. As the ACL can fluctuate from day to day, the ACL which is current at any time would have to be ascertained from the council.

section.title: Housing Association Grant
section.p: Mr. Frank Field: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment to what extent discretion is used in determining the amount of housing association grant available in each local authority's area; and what performance indicators are used in the exercise of the discretion.

Mr. Baldry: The Housing Corporation allocates 80 per cent. of the resources to a particular local authority area, over a three year period, in accordance with housing need, as measured by the housing needs indicator (HNI). The remaining 20 per cent. is distributed in the light of particular local circumstances, including the value for money of projects submitted by housing associations. Local priorities are discussed between housing authorities and the regional offices of the Housing Corporation before decisions are taken.

section.title: Water Disconnections
section.p: Mr. Frank Field: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what steps he will take to make it unlawful for water companies or others to cause a disconnection of a consumer's water supply.

Mr. Maclean: None. It is right that bills should be paid, but equally that companies should deal sympathetically with customers who are having difficulty meeting their bills. The Director General of Water Services is responsible for protecting customers' interests. He has expressed his concern over the level of disconnections, and issued guidance to water companies last year on the subject of debt and disconnection to ensure they take a consistent and fair approach towards customers with unpaid charges. The Director General is in addition proposing to carry out research to find out more about the reasons people are disconnected. The Government welcome the actions he is taking.

section.title: Tenants Charter
section.p: Ms. Corston: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment how many copies of the full council tenants charter have been requested from his Department.

Mr. Baldry: Copies of the full tenants charter were sent to all local housing authorities, housing organisations, citizens advice bureaux and law centres. In addition, over 200,000 copies of the English and ethnic language versions of the full council tenants charter have been directly requested from my Department, mainly by tenants.
Ms. Corston: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment how many copies of the full tenants charter were printed in each language; and at what cost.

Mr. Baldry: One million copies of the English language version of the full tenants charter have been printed at a cost of £123,176. Five thousand copies of each of the five ethnic language versions (Hindi, Greek, Vietnamese, Bengali and Urdu) have been printed at a cost of £41,422.

section.title: Drinking Water
section.p: Mr. Bayley: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will list the legislation or regulations requiring that information regarding the quality of drinking water is made available to the public by the water companies.

Mr. Maclean: Regulation 30 of The Water Supply (Water Quality) Regulations 1989, SI No. 1147, requires that a water undertaker shall make available for inspection by the public at all reasonable hours and free of charge, at such of its offices as are normally open to the public, and record maintained by it in accordance with regulation 29. This includes for each water supply zone, its name, the supplying water treatment works, its population, particulars of any relaxation granted or undertakings given in respect of the water supply in the zone and particulars of the result of analyses of samples taken in accordance with other parts of the Water Supply (Water Quality) Regulations.

In addition, regulation 31 requires water undertakers to prepare for publication an annual report in accordance with the terms of that regulation. A copy must be sent to the local authority for each area in which it supplies water.

section.title: Direct Labour Organisations
section.p: Mr. David Shaw: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will make a statement on the methods used to monitor direct labour organisations and the publication of comparability studies showing performance indicators of efficiency, effectiveness, employment and value for money in respect of each local authority.

Mr. Robin Squire: Local authorities carrying out work within an activity defined under the Local Government Planning and Land Act 1980 or the Local Government Act 1988 are required to keep accounts and to meet a financial objective set by my right hon. and learned Friend. They are also required to submit annual reports on these matters to my right hon. and learned Friend who considers in each case whether there are grounds for exercising his sanction powers. The introduction of local government performance indicators is a key feature in this Government's determination to raise the standard of public services. I believe that the methods adopted by the Audit Commission will enable the citizen to judge the performance of their local council in comparison with those of a similar background.

section.title: Tenants
section.p: Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will publish the responses received by his Department to the consultation paper "Compensation for Tenants' Improvements".

Sir George Young: Some 61 responses to the consultation paper have been received to date. A list of the respondents has been placed in the Library of the House. The responses will be held for six months in the Department's central library.

section.title: Local Government Finance
section.p: Mr. Heppell: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what is the ratio of expenditure on administration to total expenditure for (a) county councils and (b) shire district councils; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Robin Squire: The budgeted ratio of expenditure on general administration (not allocated to other services) to total expenditure on services (both measured net of sales, fees and charges) in 1992–93 was 0·3 per cent. in county councils and 3 per cent. in shire district councils.

section.title: Housing
section.p: 116. Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will publish responses to the consultation paper draft explanatory note on planning and affordable housing.
Sir George Young: We will place copies in the Library of the House of Commons once we have finished considering them and have issued a final version of the guidance.

section.title: Council Leaseholders
section.p: 117. Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what action he has taken to assist council leaseholders.

Sir George Young: The Government legislated in 1986 to meet concerns over high service charges on flats sold under the right to buy. Purchasers now have binding estimates of the maximum charges for repairs and improvements during the first five years of the lease, and the right to a loan for particularly high charges.
Leaseholders have nevertheless reported difficulties over service charges and over resale. The Department is looking into these with landlords and the Council of Mortgage Lenders.

section.title: Housing, Tower Hamlets
section.p: 120. Mr. Peter Shore: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment how many public sector dwellings were started and completed by the Tower Hamlets local authority and by housing associations in Tower Hamlets in each year since 1986.

Mr. Baldry: Estimates of housebuilding starts and completions by sector in Tower Hamlets for each year from 1986 to 1991 and for the first half of 1992 are shown in the October 1992 edition of "Local Housing Statistics" (issue No. 103), tables 1(b) to 1(h). A copy of this publication is in the Library.

section.title: Substandard Accommodation
section.p: 121. Mrs. Dunwoody: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what percentage of (a) Asian and (b) white households live in substandard accommodation; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Baldry: This information is not available.

section.title: Inner City Projects, Coventry
section.p: 124. Mr. Jim Cunningham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will list the total amount of grants for inner city projects in Coventry given in each of the last five years.
125. Mr. Jim Cunningham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what proposals he has received for schemes for inner city projects in Coventry which he does not propose to fund.

Mr. Robin Squire: We have received a number of proposals from Coventry along with other local authorities of support for inner city projects which we have not been able to assist. Clearly we do not have unlimited funds. However it is open to local authorities to support such projects through use of their capital receipts and any private sector or other contributions.

section.title: Inner City Policies
section.p: 126. Mr. Jim Cunningham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will place in the Library the reviews that have been undertaken by his Department on the operation of the Government's inner city policies.

Mr. Robin Squire: My Department has carried out a number of evaluations of its various programmes for urban areas including, most recently, the achievements of three of the inner cities task forces; relevant reports are in the Library. Further details of my Department's urban policies and programmes are in the 1993 DOE annual report published 10 February.

section.title: Local Government Commission
section.p: 128. Mr. Heppell: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) if he will set out the full proposed timetable for the second tranche of the work of the Local Government Commission;
(2) what steps he is taking to ensure that all local authorities are given adequate advance warning of the start time of the local government review in their area;
(3) if he will make it his policy not to require the Local Government Commission to begin any review in the period immediately before or immediately after the 1993 local elections.
Mr. Robin Squire: In reply to a question from my hon. Friend the Member for the Isle of Wight (Mr. Field), my
Mr. Robin Squire: This Department has provided the following inner cities grants to Coventry in the last five years:

hon. Friend the Minister of State for Local Government and Inner Cities announced on 4 February the timetable for the Local Government Commission's second tranche reviews, and placed a copy in the House Library.

All local authorities in the areas in the second tranche were sent a copy of the announcement, together with the timetable. This gives them a minimum of three months to prepare their initial submissions to the commission.

The Secretary of State intends to direct the commission to begin the first review in the second tranche on 10 May 1993, immediately after the county council elections. There is no need to delay the beginning of the reviews any further.

section.title: Homelessness
section.p: 129. Mrs. Dunwoody: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what percentages of (a) ethnic minorities and (b) white people are homeless in London.

Mr. Baldry: Local authorities report the number of households for whom they accept responsibility to secure permanent accommodation under the homelessness provisions of the Housing Act 1985 in their quarterly P1(E) return.

In the quarter ending September 1992 only 17 out of 33 London boroughs provided the information classified by ethnic origin. On average in those boroughs 47 per cent. of households accepted as homeless were from ethnic minorities and 53 per cent. were white.

section.title: Housing Associations
section.p: Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will publish the Hambros report into the actuarial margin of risk of private sector borrowing by housing associations.
Sir George Young: I refer the hon. Gentleman to the answer I gave to the hon. Member for Greenwich (Mr. Raynsford) on Monday 18 January at column 113.

135. Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what assessment he has made of the change
275 in the share of housing association programmes dedicated to rehabilitation of existing stock; and if he will make a statement.

Sir George Young: The Department has commissioned research into the amount of rehabilitation work undertaken by housing associations. The first part of the research, undertaken by PIEDA plc in association with Rodney Dykes Housing Services Ltd, was published at the end of January. I have arranged for copies to be placed in the Library of the House.

The results show that there are a number of factors which have resulted in fewer dwellings being rehabilitated by housing associations than in the past. In addition to the changes brought about by the new financial regime, introduced by the Housing Act 1988, they include: the availability of cheaper land relative to the acquisition costs of properties in need of repair, which encourages new build; increasing opportunities for off-the-shelf purchases of new dwellings from private builders; and the drying up of suitable properties available for rehabilitation in some areas.

The Department has recently let a contract for the second part of the research, which will examine the effects of the decline. The research will again be undertaken by PIEDA, which is due to report in December this year. In the meantime, I have asked the Housing Corporation to aim to maintain rehabat at least at its current level.

section.title: Local Authority Housing
section.p: 140. Mr. Peter Shore: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment how many local authority dwellings were reported as vacant in the London borough of Tower Hamlets in 1992; what percentage of the local authority housing stock this figure respresents; and what is the comparable percentage in other London boroughs.

Mr. Robin Squire: Local authorities report the numbers of their own dwellings that are vacant in their annual housing investment programme (HIP1) returns. At 1 April 1992 Tower Hamlets reported 1,703 of their dwellings as empty, 4·2 per cent. of their dwelling stock. The comparable percentage for the other London boroughs is 2·3 per cent.

section.title: House Completions, Leicester
section.p: Mr. Janner: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment how many houses were completed in Leicester in 1979, 1989 and 1992 respectively.
Mr. Baldry: The total number of housebuilding completions in the city of Leicester local authority area in 1979 was 1,247, in 1989, 227 and for 1992, provisionally, 534.

section.title: Uniform Business Rate
section.p: Mr. Henderson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment when the next uniform business rate revaluation is due to take place.
Mr. Robin Squire: New rating lists will be compiled on 1 April 1995 based on 1 April 1993 values.

Mr. Henderson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the sum paid by British Coal in uniform business rates for 1992 (a) in total and (b) in respect of the 31 pits due for closure.
Mr. Robin Squire: Information on the rates paid by British Coal is not held centrally by the Government.

section.title: English Nature
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what guidance he has given to English Nature concerning its obligation to disseminate to the public data and information on the state of the environment; and what steps are being taken by English Nature to advertise its new responsibilities relating to the provision of environmental information.

Mr. Maclean: English Nature already disseminates information on nature conservation as one of its key functions. My Department has provided guidance on the new Environmental Information Regulations which took effect in December and English Nature will be taking steps to inform its customers and partners of how it intends to meet its obligations under the regulations.

section.title: Environmental Data
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will instruct the Joint Nature Conservation Committee to institute a system to ensure that enviornmental data or information disseminated by English Nature, Scottish Natural Heritage or the Countryside Council for Wales are made available in a mutually consistent form.
Mr. Maclean: No. This is a matter for the committee to consider in consultation with the three councils.

section.title: Parliament Square (Air Quality)
section.p: Mr. Alfred Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, pursuant to his answer of 10 January, Official Report, columns 654–55, what is the nearest point to Parliament square, Westminster, for which he has records of air quality; and if he will undertake a sample survey of air quality in Parliament square.

Mr. Maclean: The site nearest to Parliament square at which air quality is monitored is at Bridge place, Victoria. The Department has no plans to undertake air quality monitoring in Parliament square.

section.title: Darwin Initiative
section.p: Mr. Milligan: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will make a statement on the Advisory Committee on the Darwin Initiative and indicate its membership.

Mr. Howard: The Prime Minister signed the convention on biological diversity in Rio de Janiero at the UN conference on environment and development. In order to support the aims of the convention he launched at that time the Darwin initiative for the survival of species. The initiative aims to deploy British scientific, managerial and commercial strengths in biodiversity to assist with the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity and natural habitats.

In December a consultation paper was issued to a wide variety of individuals, organisations and individuals seeking views on the scope of the initiative and ideas for projects which might meet the initiative's objectives. I announced at that time that I intended to establish an
277 advisory committee on the Darwin initiative. This committee will have regard to the work already in progress on biodiversity and the available resources, and will make recommendations on the areas on which the Darwin initiative should initially be targeted, the relative priority to be given to different programmes, and the financial support to be made available to them. Sir Crispin Tickell has agreed to be chairman of that committee, and I am pleased to announce that the other members of the committee are: Ms. Janet Barber, Dr. Brian Bayne FIBiol, Dr. Eileen Buttle FIBiol, Mr. Robin Herbert DL JP, David Horrobin, professor Robert May FRS and Sir David Smith FRS FRSE. The committee held its first meeting on 15 February.

section.title: Olympic Bid
section.p: Mr. Sumberg: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what progress has been made on the Manchester 2000 Olympic bid; and if he will make a statement on Government support.

Mr. Howard: The details of the formal bid submitted by the Manchester Olympic Bid Committee to the International Olympic Committee will be made public today. I am arranging for a copy of the candidature file and the executive summary to be placed in the Library of the House.

My hon. Friend the Minister for Local Government and Inner Cities previously announced on Tuesday 26 January—Official Report column 600—that the Government are providing up to £75 million to support the bid in advance of the IOC's decision on the nomination. In addition, the candidature file sets out the undertakings made by the Government if Manchester is successful. In particular, the Government will ensure that all the necessary facilities will be built, partly by private finance and partly by substantial public funding. We also intend to legislate at the earliest opportunity following the IOC's nomination of Manchester to ensure that the Organising Committee for the Games has the necessary powers to plan and implement this event. The Government are backing wholeheartedly Manchester's bid for the 2000 Olympic Games.

section.title: London Boroughs (Debt)
section.p: Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what assistance he proposes to make available to London boroughs and the Common Council during 1993–94 in respect of extra costs due to his decisions on housing revenue account subsidy in respect of debt inherited from the former Greater London Council; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Redwood: It is my right hon. Friend's firm intention to issue capitalisation directions and supplementary credit approvals (SCAs) to authorities facing during 1993–94 extra costs due to his decision that housing revenue account subsidy is not payable under the statute in respect of certain debts inherited from the former Greater London council. The court yesterday upheld this decision.

Authorities which face such extra costs will be able to apply for capitalisation directions and SCAs during a period which my right hon. Friend intends to specify and which will not be shorter than six months from yesterday when the court gave its judgment.

In deciding the amount of a direction and SCA to issue to an authority, my right hon. Friend intends to have regard inter alia to the resources available to him under the Government's public expenditure plans, the authority's 1993–94 budget—in particular the scope for the authority to accommodate the extra costs within that budget, and to the financial reserves and useable capital receipts available to the authority. To the extent that costs are covered by directions and SCAs their impact on the council tax is spread over a number of years.

I am arranging for London boroughs and the Common Council to be sent today the details of the scheme for issuing these directions and SCAs which my right hon. Friend intends to adopt. Authorities will need to take account of these intentions when setting their 1993–94 budgets.

section.title: River Pollution
section.p: Mr. Mullin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment (1) what assessment his Department has made of the impact of the closure of pits in the Durham coalfield on the pollution of the River Wear and other local waterways;

(2) what response he has made to the report on the probable environmental impact of the closure of Vane Tempest and Easington collieries by Dr. Paul Younger of Newcastle university; and what steps he is taking to avoid pollution of the River Wear.

Mr. Maclean [holding answer 15 February 1993]: None. It is for British Coal and the National Rivers Authority, in the first place, to assess the environmental effects of pit closures and any relevant reports on the subject, and to consider what action may need to be taken to avoid pollution. My officials and the staff of the NRA have been in frequent contact about pollution from closed mines, and arrangements have been made between British Coal and the NRA for effective liaison over any proposed pit closures.

section.title: Unified Housing Waiting Lists
section.p: Mr. George Howarth: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will hold talks with the National Federation of Housing Associations, the Association of Metropolitan Authorities and the Association of district councils to discuss the establishment of unified housing waiting lists between local authorities and housing associations.

Mr. Baldry [holding answer 12 February 1993]: My Department held a seminar which discussed the subject last year; attendance included representatives of the organisations mentioned. We are considering holding a further seminar to review developments.

section.title: Audit Commission (Lambeth)
section.p: Mr. Fraser: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what reports he has received from the Audit Commission that arising out of the discharge of its own duties it has discovered substantial fraud, corruption or other crimes, or substantial ultra vires expenditure, in Lambeth.

Mr. Robin Squire [holding answer 16 February 1993]: Neither the Audit Commission nor the auditor report to
279 my right hon. and learned Friend: they perform their duties independently. I understand, however, that Lambeth's auditor is preparing a report which will deal with allegations of fraud, corruption and related matters.

section.title: Seven Estuary (Pollution)
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the total annual discharge into the Severn estuary from English counties of (a) ammonia, (b) cadmium, (c) lead, (d) copper, (e) chromium, )f) cyanide, (g) nickel, (h) mercury and (i) zince in the latest year for which figures are available.

Mr. Maclean [holding answer 16 February 1993]: The information requested is not held centrally. Details of maximum authorised loads contained in relevant discharge consents, and related water quality monitoring results for the Severn estuary, are available on public registers in the National Rivers Authority regions concerned.

section.title: Minewater Pumping
section.p: Mr. Cousins: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what discussion he has had with the National Rivers Authority about the consequences of stopping minewater pumping in the Tyneside area.

Mr. MacLean[holding answer 19 January 1993]: My right hon. Friend and I have not discussed this specific matter with the National Rivers Authority. It is for British Coal and the NRA, in the first place, to assess any environmental consquences of stopping minewater pumping.

section.title: Drivers (Criminal Convictions)
section.p: 109. Ms. Walley: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what research he has conducted into the extent to which drivers seeking licences to drive hackney carriages and private hire carriages have failed to disclose information relating to (a) rape offences and (b) other criminal convictions; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Freeman: I have been asked to reply.

No such research has been undertaken. Outside London, district councils issue licences to drive hackney carriages and private hire vehicles and since 1 April 1992 they have been able to request a police check of the possible criminal record of applicants for licences. Only each individual council, after obtaining criminal record details, would be able to gauge the extent to which licence holders had failed to disclose previous convictions. I do not believe there is any need to hold such information centrally.

119. Ms. Walley: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what proposals he has to ensure that licences to drive hackney carriages and private hire vehicles are not issued to men with criminal records which include rape.
Mr. Freeman: I have been asked to reply.

Section 47 of the Road Traffic Act 1991 gives local authorities a power to check with the police if applicants for hackney carriage and PHV drivers' licences have any criminal convictions. A copy of the guidance issued to police and local authorities last year on how the vetting arrangements should operate was placed in the House of Commons Library.

District councils must decide, on the basis of all the information at their disposal, whether an applicant is a fit and proper person to hold such a licence. They should not take into account any convictions which are "spent" by virtue of the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974.

section.title: Justices of the Peace
section.p: Mr. Hoon: To ask the Parliamentary Secretary, Lord Chancellor's Department how many (a) women and (b) members of ethnic minorities have been appointed as justices of the peace in Nottinghamshire since 1989.

Mr. John M. Taylor: Since 1989, 151 persons have been appointed as justices of the peace in Nottinghamshire. Of that number there were 74 females and eight members of ethnic minorities—four males and four females.

section.title: Statutory Instruments
section.p: Ms. Corston: To ask the Parliamentary Secretary, Lord Chancellor's Department how many statutory instruments were laid before Parliament by his Department in each year since 1980.
Mr. John M. Taylor: The information requested could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Palestine Liberation Organisation
section.p: Mr. David Evans: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will make it his policy to continue to decline to hold meetings at ministerial level with the leaders of the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Mr. Douglas Hogg: I refer my hon. Friend to the answer I gave the hon. Member for Glasgow, Hillhead (Mr. Galloway) on 10 February, at column 680.

section.title: Ozone-depleting Substances
section.p: Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how many chlorofluorocarbon and hydrochlorofluorocarbon installations are contained within his Department's buildings.
Mr. Goodlad: Four hundred and thirty nine.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how much funding has been allocated or spent specifically to deal with measures to reduce his Department's consumption of ozone-depleting substances.

Mr. Goodlad: The Department has allocated £75,000 in the 1993–94 financial year for absorption chiller plant to reduce its use of CFCs/HCFCs, and £157,000 on high-frequency lighting to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how many refrigeration and air conditioning system in the Department are equipped with automatic leak detection systems.
Mr. Goodlad: None.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how the departmental green Minister has promoted protection of the ozone layer with specific policy measures; which possible measures have been considered and rejected; and on what grounds.

Mr. Goodlad: The green Ministers for the Department continue to promote protection of the ozone layer through active FCO involvement in international environmental policy, the planned reduction of energy consumption in the Department and the reduction of use of ozone-depleting substances.
Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs which current uses of ozone-depleting chemicals by his Department are considered essential.
Mr. Goodlad: The Department is advised that the only ozone-depleting chemicals considered essential are those in inhalants supplied to posts overseas for medicinal purposes.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs by what date his Department's use of ozone-depleting chemicals will conform to EC regulations on limits on these chemicals.

Mr. Goodlad: The Department is advised that it is only the production and supply of new ozone-depleting substances which must conform to EC Regulations. The Department will, however, reduce its use of ozone-depleting substances as soon as practicable.
Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what targets have been set for the recycling of ozone-depleting chemicals within Departmental buildings.
Mr. Goodlad: None. Information is currently being compiled to enable targets to be set.
Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how many chlorofluorocarbon domestic fridges are contained within his Department's buildings.
Mr. Goodlad: Three hundred and sixty-seven.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how many catastrophic leaks of ozone-depleting substances have occurred within his Department's buildings on the last five years.
Mr. Goodlad: None.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what measures have been taken to ensure that ozone-destroying substances in use by his Department identified as controlled waste under the Environmental Protection Act 1990 do not reach the atmosphere.
Mr. Goodlad: Equipment containing ozone-depleting substances is returned to the manufacturers for recycling.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will give an undertaking to purchase only ozone-friendly fridges that do not contain chlorofluorocarbons or hydrochlorofluorocarbons for his Department.
Mr. Goodlad: The Department does not purchase fridges containing CFCs or HCFCs where acceptable alternatives offering value for money are available.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what guidance has been sought and received on alternatives or substitutes to the ozone-destroying chemicals in use by his Department.

Mr. Goodlad: In 1992, the Department appointed a firm of consultants to carry out a programme of environmental audits of its home estate. A primary purpose of the audits was to seek advice on alternatives or substitutes to the ozone-destroying chemicals in use in the Department. The consultants are due to report shortly.

Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commowealth Affairs how many portable halon fire extinguishers are contained within Departmental buildings; and what measures are being taken to ensure their recycling and replacement.
Mr. Goodlad: One hundred and forty-five. They will be replaced this year and returned to the manufacturers for recycling.

section.title: Kashmir
section.p: Mr. Cox: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs when a United Kingdom Government Minister last visited the Indian-controlled area of Kashmir; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Lennox-Boyd: I am not aware that any official visits have been made by United Kingdom Government Ministers to Kashmir in recent years.

Mr. Cox: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what discussion he has had with the Pakistan Government as to possible aid from Her Majesty's Government to help resettle Kashmiri people who have fled from the Indian-controlled area of Kashmir; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Lennox-Boyd: We have had no discussion with the Pakistan Government about helping to resettle Kashmiris.

section.title: Birmingham Summit
section.p: Dr. Lynne Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs, pursuant to his answer of 5 February, official Report, column 393, what subheads of what votes will be used to meet the cost of the Birmingham summit; and how these costs were apportioned.

Mr. Garel-Jones The costs of the Birmingham European summit were met as follows:
£ million
FCO vote 1, subhead A 1 (1) 2.3
Home Office vote 1, subhead D1. Specific grant at 51 per cent, of the additional policing costs 0.8

section.title: Eastern Europe
section.p: Mr. Streeter: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what plans he has to open new posts in the independent states of the former Soviet Union and in eastern Europe; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Hurd: I am pleased to announce that we shall be opening three new embassies in the former Soviet Union and eastern Europe. They will be in Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan; Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan; and Bratislava, the capital of Slovakia. All of these countries are going through an important and difficult process of political and economic change. We want to be in the best position to help and encourage the development of democratic societies pursuing liberal economic policies and to promote trade and investment. In the case of both Baku and Tashkent, we are responding to direct requests from British industry to open embassies in each place.
This decision has been made possible by savings in support areas at home and overseas.

section.title: Radiation Workers
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will make it his policy to introduce a no fault compensation scheme for radiation workers employed by or contracted to his Department similar to the scheme adopted by British Nuclear Fuels and the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority.

Mr. Aitken: Consideration is being given to the introduction of radiation compensation arrangements similar in effect to those of the civil nuclear industry. The possibility of my Department's membership of, or association with, the BNFL/AEA scheme is under discussion with the industry and the trade unions.

section.title: Mr. Rudi Molinari
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence how much his Department spent on legal fees for participation in the court case involving the claim for compensation by Mr. Rudi Molinari, a former employee at the royal dockyard at Chatham, against his Department for damage claimed to have been received from radiation exposure at the shipyard.
Mr. Aitken: This case is the subject of continuing legal proceedings and the costs are not yet known.

section.title: Helicopter Carrier Ship
section.p: Mr. Ronnie Campbell: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will outline the programme for the procurement of the helicopter carrier ship.
Mr. Aitken: I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave on 9 February, Official Report, column 574.

section.title: Statutory Instruments
section.p: Ms. Corston: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence how many statutory instruments were laid before Parliament by his Department in each year since 1980.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: The information requested is as follows:

section.title: Contracting Out
section.p: Mr. McAllion: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will provide figures for the reduction in numbers of posts as a result of contracting out since 1979 in his Department and agencies for which he has responsibility.
Mr. Aitken: We estimate that, since 1979, competition for defence support services has resulted in a reduction of 18,000 posts in my Department and in the agencies for which we are responsible.

section.title: Armed Forces (Sexual Behaviour)
section.p: Mr. Michael Brown: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence what proposals he has for the regulation of inappropriate sexual behaviour between heterosexual members of the armed forces; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: Service personnel are made aware of the standards of behaviour required and that inappropriate sexual behaviour of any kind can lead to administrative or disciplinary action. Inappropriate sexual conduct of a heterosexual nature by members of the armed forces is dealt with under existing service regulations.

Mr. Michael Brown: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will bring forward proposals governing the conduct of British troops serving with homosexual armed forces personnel in combined NATO or UN peacekeeping forces; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: British Armed Forces personnel are well aware of the standards of behaviour expected of them and the consequences of any misconduct, heterosexual, homosexual or otherwise. We have no plans, therefore, to introduce regulations specific to those serving with NATO or UN peace-keeping forces alongside homosexual personnel of other armed forces.

section.title: MFV Pescado
section.p: 99. Ms Walley: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence if he will deploy Royal Navy facilities to raise the MFV Pescado.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: The raising of the MFV Pescado is a matter for the civil authorities. Any request for assistance would, however, be given careful consideration.

section.title: Traffic Calming
section.p: Mr. Mans: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport when consultation on regulations under the Traffic Calming Act 1992 is to start.

Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: Commencing today, the Department of Transport and the Welsh Office are consulting widely on draft regulations with the local authority associations and other interested parties. We aim to draw the consultation to a close before Easter.

section.title: MV Goldeneye
section.p: Ms. Walley: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport if he will make a statement on the reasons for awarding MV Goldeneye a load line exemption certificate; what is the registration of MV Goldeneye; and if he will carry out a port state control inspection of MV Goldeneye.
Mr. Norris: The owners of the unregistered salvage vessel Goldeneye applied for a load line exemption certificate which was issued after survey by a Department surveyor.
The ship is subject to inspection at any time arid arrangements will be made accordingly within the inspection programme.

section.title: Railway Privatisation
section.p: Mr. Bayley: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport (1) what is the date by which comments were sought on his Department's consultative document "Railway Privatisation: A Voice for the Passengers"; and when copies of this document were made available in the Vote Office;

(2) how many copies of his Department's consultative document "Railway Privatisation: A Voice for the Passenger" were printed; and how and when these documents were made available to British Rail passengers.

Mr. Freeman: The document was published on 16 December 1992 and 2,000 copies were printed. It was placed in the Vote Office the same day and copies were sent to bodies likely to have an interest in the future of the consultative committees. The availability of the document was publicised in a press notice and copies have been provided free of charge on request. The requested reply date for comments was 22 January 1993.

section.title: Zebra Crossings
section.p: Mr. Cox: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport how many pedestrians have been hit by a motor vehicle while crossing a zebra crossing in England and Wales during the year 1992.
Mr. Kenneth Carlisle: Data are not yet available for 1992. There were 1,673 pedestrians injured by motor vehicles on zebra crossings in 1991 in England and Wales.

section.title: Oil Tankers
section.p: Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport what immediate steps he proposes to take to improve safety regulations on oil tankers within British waters.

Mr. Norris [holding answer 12 February 1993]: Regulations governing tankers are under constant review within the International Maritime Organisation. The Department is at the forefront of these discussions and developments.

In addition, an initiative has been taken by national and international organisations concerned with tanker operations to develop a voluntary code with regard to tanker routeing around the United Kingdom coast. They have also given an undertaking to re-emphasise to masters the need to pay greater attention to passage planning and to provide early advice to coastal states when tankers are experiencing problems which affect their navigation.

section.title: Radio Transponders
section.p: Mr. Wallace: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport on how many occasions since 1 January 1988 Ministers and officials of his Department have taken part in meetings of the International Maritime Organisation or its committees to discuss the subject of fitting radio transponders on vessels.

Mr. Norris [holding answer 16 February 1993]: Department officials have taken part in four meetings of the sub-committee on safety of navigation and one meeting of the sub-committee on radiocommunications at the International Maritime Organisation since 1 January 1988 with regard to developing radio transponders for use on vessels.

section.title: Vessel Inspections
section.p: Mr. Wallace: To ask the Secretary of State for Transport how many port state inspections of vessels have been undertaken by officials of his Department at (a) Sullom Voe and (b) Flotta in each year since 1990 and in January 1993; and what percentage of vessels visiting these respective ports the numbers constitute.

Mr. Norris [holding answer 16 February 1993: The directors of marine at Sullom Voe and Flotta carry out their own vetting procedure of visiting ships and alert the Department if they are concerned by the condition of a visiting ship.
In addition the number of port state control inspections undertaken at Sullom Voe and Flotta for the years in question is given in the table.
These inspections constituted the following percentages of individual foreign ships which visited these ports.

section.title: Overseas Political Organisations
section.p: Mr. Hunter: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department in what circumstances he would take steps to prevent political organisations of other countries from maintaining offices in the United Kingdom.

Mr. Jack: People in this country are free to engage in what political activities they like, including working for foreign political organisations, provided of course that their activities remain within the law.

section.title: Devon and Cornwall Police
section.p: Mr. Steen: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, pursuant to his answer of 8 February, Official Report, column 439, how many recruits began service with the Devon and Cornwall constabulary on 7 December 1992.
Mr. Charles Wardle: Sixteen recruits began service with the Devon and Cornwall constabulary on 7 December 1992.

section.title: Royal Commission on Criminal Justice
section.p: Mr. Dowd: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when the report of the Royal Commission on criminal justice is due to be completed; and when he expects to publish it.
Mr. Jack: The Royal Commission on criminal justice hopes to complete its report by the end of June. The report will be published as soon thereafter as printing schedules allow.

section.title: Data Protection
section.p: Mr. Cohen: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how the Council for Europe convention on data protection provides a framework for harmonisation of European Community data protection laws.

Mr. Charles Wardle: The Council of Europe convention for the protection of individuals with regard to automatic processing of personal data prescribes the basic principles which have to be observed in handling personal data within states party to the convention. Accession to the convention by all European Community member states, and the enactment of the necessary domestic legislation to give effect to the convention's requirements, would thus provide for a consistent data protection regime within the Community.

section.title: Children's Rights
section.p: Mr. Alton: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (I) if he will introduce legislation to give United Kingdom courts jurisdiction to try British nationals and residents for sexual offences against children abroad; and if he will make a statement;
(2) what measures the British Government are taking to comply with article 34 of the United Nations convention on the rights of the child.

Mr. Jack: The Government wholly support the principles set out in the United Nations convention on the rights of the child, which we ratified in 1991. Our law against the sexual abuse and exploitation of children is rightly severe.

We have no plans, however, to extend the largely territorial jurisdiction of our courts to deal with offences committed abroad against children; nor is there any requirement for us to do so in order to fulfil our obligations under article 34 of the convention. Where such offences have been committed abroad it is for the country concerned to enforce its own law. We are always ready, however, to assist through extradition and by giving legal assistance under the Criminal Justice (International Co-operation) Act 1990.

section.title: Sex Tourism
section.p: Mr. Alton: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what action the British Government have taken to discourage the promotion of sex tourism through holiday brochures, magazines and other forms of mass communications in this country.

Mr. Jack: While the Government have no power to ban or censor publications, anyone publishing brochures promoting sex tourism could risk prosecution under the Obscene Publications Act 1959, or for an offence of conspiracy to corrupt public morals at common law. It would, however, be for the courts to decide whether an offence had been committed in any individual case.

section.title: Crime Statistics
section.p: Mr. Blair: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what percentage of notifiableoffences were cleared up in (a) 1990, (b) 1991 and (c) July 1991 to June 1992, in each offence category and for each police force region.

Mr. Jack: The requested information for 1990 is published in table 2·22 of "Criminal Statistics, England and Wales 1990," a copy of which is available in the Library. Information for 1991 is published in the table. Information for the 12 months to June 1992 is not available.

td.i: Notifiable offences recorded by the police: clear-up rate by offence group and police force area

tr.td: 1 Excluding offences of "other criminal damage" of value £20 and under.
2 Offences cleared up in current year may have been initially recorded in an earlier year.

section.p: Mr. Sweeney: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what information he has as to the police manpower levels, crime statistics and clear-up rates of police forces in (a) England and Wales and (h) other EC countries.

Mr. Charles Wardle: The police forces of England and Wales provide monthly statistical returns of strength for police officers and civilian support staff. Information on notifiable offences recorded by the police and clear-up 292 rates is collected on a regular basis and the statistics are published half-yearly in a Home Office statistical bulletin and annually in the Command Paper "Criminal Statistics: England and Wales".
Comparable statistical data on police service complementing or crime rates for member states of the EC are not available.

section.title: Obscenity
section.p: Mrs. Ann Winterton: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, pursuant to his answer of 5 February to the hon. Member for Castle Point (Dr. Spink) Official Report, column 350, if he will indicate the precise terms in which he is currently consulting about the subject of obscenity; if he will make it his policy to include an invitation to comment on the provisions of the Obscene Publications Act 1959 as distinct from the means of its enforcement; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Jack: I have asked my officials to consider, in consultation with other parties, whether improvements might be made in the enforcement of the Obscene Publications Acts 1959 and 1964, and other legislation relating to obscenity. I have not asked them to invite wider comment on the provisions of the Obscene Publications Act 1959, although as I indicated in my reply to my hon. Friend the Member for Castle Point, 1 am receiving representations relating to the Act, which I keep under review.

section.title: Ecstasy
section.p: Mr. Richards: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many people have died from the use of the drug Ecstasy; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Jack: This information is not collected centrally.

section.title: Ram Raiding
section.p: Mr. Richards: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what measures are being taken to alert businesses to the threat of ram raiding.

Mr. Jack: In areas where ram raiding is a problem, the local police are able to alert businesses to the risks and, drawing on their own experience and the expertise of the Home Office crime prevention centre at Stafford, they are always ready to give specialist advice on what measures the owners can take to protect their premises against this type of offence.

section.title: Bosnian Refugees
section.p: Mr. Allen: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many refugees from Bosnia have arrived in each EC country; and how many are expected in the next six months.

Mr. Charles Wardle: In the period January 1992 to January 1993 inclusive around 5,900 nationals of the former Yugoslavia, excluding dependants, have applied for asylum in the United Kingdom. The large majority of these applications are still under consideration and the applicants are being allowed to stay in the meantime. More detailed data on the origin of the applicants are not available.

In addition, as I announced to the House on 30 November 1992, we are willing to accept 1,000 ex-detainees from Bosnia and other parts of the former Yugoslavia, together with their dependants, totalling perhaps 4,000 in all. The first two groups have already arrived.
The available information on applicants to other EC member states is given in the table.
It is not feasible to make a forecast of future applications, in view of the uncertainties.

td.i: by nationals of the former Yugoslavia to certain other EC member states from around mid 1991 to the latter part of 1992

section.title: Deaths in Custody
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what action he intends to take on the suggestion in the report of the Ashworth special hospital inquiry 1992, chaired by Sir Louis Blom Cooper, that the Government should make a modest contribution annually to the organisation Inquest to allow it to represent those who die in legal custody.
Mr. Peter Lloyd [holding answer 15 February 1993]: The Government have no plans to contribute to the funding of the organisation Inquest.

section.title: Research and Development
section.p: Mr. Cousins: To ask the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster what is the expenditure on (a) the second framework research and development programme 1987 to 1991 and (b) the third framework research and development programme from 1990 to1994 in total and broken down by programme area; what is the share of spend in each programme by the United Kingdom and Germany in total and for each programme area; and if he will express the figures in pound sterling and in ecus.

Mr. Waldegrave: The second EC framework programme, adopted on 28 September 1987, amounted to 5·396 billion ecu—£4·088 billion at current exchange rates—and was distributed between the main programme areas as set out in table A.

The third EC framework programme, adopted on 23 April 1990, amounted to 5·7 billion ecu—£4·318 billion —and the Council reached a common orientation for a supplement of 900 million ecu—£682 million—on 31 December 1992. The funds will be allocated between the main areas of research as set out in table B.

EC research programmes under the overlapping frameworks are managed mainly by directorates general XII and XIII of the European Commission. Information on the share of funds awarded to research organisations in member states, in the form of shared cost contracts, has been derived from Commission statistics for the period 1987–1991. For this purpose the Commission has grouped
295 the specific research programmes of the second framework programme in the same format as the third framework programme, and its analysis includes all contracts awarded after 1986, including some made under the first framework programme of 1984–87.

The difference between total contract expenditure of 3,038·78 million ecu in table C and the overall amount agreed for the second framework programme of 5,396 million ecu in table A includes expenditure on other mechanisms for developing Community research, such as concerted actions, conferences, workshops, publications, direct research activities at the joint research centre, fusion research, and sums yet to be committed.

The funds under the first and second framework programmes awarded to United Kingdom and German research organisations between 1987–1991 are summarised by programme, according to Commission statistics, in table C. A full statistical table showing funds awarded to all member states will be placed in the Library.
Because of delays in implementation, only preliminary statistics are available for the third framework programme. These are set out in table D.

section.title: Contracting Out
section.p: Mr. McAllion: To ask the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster if he will provide figures for the reduction in number of posts as a result of contracting out since 1979 in his Department and agencies for which he has responsibility.
Mr. Waldegrave: This information is not available except at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Public Record Office
section.p: Dr. Wright: To ask the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster what representations he has recently received about the release of specific retained documents by the Public Record Office; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Robert Jackson: In response to my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Duchy's invitation to historians in June 1992 to inform him of blocks of closed records that should now be considered for release, he has received more than 50 representations relating to the release of such records.

section.title: Apple Juice
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will name the brands of apple juice containing high levels of patulin which have been on sale in the United Kingdom.

Mr. Soames: It is not the Department's general policy to publish details of the brands of products examined in the course of food surveillance unless there is a particular need to do so. In this case I believe it would not be helpful to publish the brands involved. The evidence we have is that, as with any naturally occurring toxicant, there is likely to be a good deal of variation in contamination levels between batches of apple juice regardless of the producer. Furthermore, the manufacturers involved have now taken steps to avoid a recurrence of the problem.

Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what assessment he has made of the danger of (a) cancer and (b) birth defects resulting from consumption of apple juice containing high levels of patulin.

Mr. Soames: There is no evidence linking the consumption of apple juice containing patulin with any cases of cancer or birth defects. However, the Department of Health has advised me that patulin has been shown to be a mutagen in both in vitro and in vivo studies in animals and should be regarded as a potential carcinogen. The
299 Department's committee on toxicity has therefore advised that patulin levels in food should be reduced to the lowest level that is technologically achievable.

section.title: Local Authorities (Employees' Remuneration)
section.p: Sir John Wheeler: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will require each local authority to publish annually the level of salary and the total remuneration package, including pension arrangements, payable to the authority's chief executive and directors.

Mr. Redwood: There is a strong case for local authorities to publish details of the pay of their senior staff in broadly the same way as companies are required to publish details of the pay of their senior employees. However, I am also keen to keep new obligations on local authorities under control.

My Department will consider what information it would be appropriate for local authorities to publish and the best way for the local authorities to be encouraged to make that information public. Of course, no new stipulations would be introduced without consultation with the local authority associations.

section.title: Environmental Technology Innovation Scheme
section.p: Mr. John Evans: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the initial three-year budget of his Department's environmental technology innovation scheme launched in October 1990; and how much has been spent to date.

Mr. Maclean: The initial budget for the environmental technology innovation scheme—ETIS—was £12 million divided equally between my Department and the Department of Trade and Industry. Of the £4·6 million so far committed by the DOE on approved projects, £1·25 million has been spent to date. These two figures include grants to projects initially submitted under DOE's predecessor scheme which was subsumed into ETIS in October 1990.
Mr. John Evans: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment when he expects to finalise the environmental technology innovation scheme budget for the next financial year.
Mr. Maclean: Provision for my Department's expenditure on grants under the scheme will be included in the main supply estimates which will be published next month.

section.title: Noise Pollution
section.p: Mr. O'Neill: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what estimates his Department has made of the level of noise pollution generated by seismic survey activity; and what studies his Department has made of the effect of noise pollution on marine life in United Kingdom coastal water.

Mr. Maclean: Seismic survey activity is usually undertaken to support oil and gas exploration and is therefore a matter for my right hon. Friend the President of the Board of Trade. My Department has recently 300 established a working group on acoustic disturbance to small cetaceans, under the chairmanship of the Natural Environment Research Council's sea mammals research unit.

section.title: Waste Shipments
section.p: Mr. Carttiss: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what progress was made during the United Kingdom presidency of the EC in regulating transfrontier shipments of waste.

Mr. Maclean: The Environment Council reached agreement on the waste shipments regulation and on a decision on the conclusion, by the Community and its member states, of the United Nations Environment Programme's Basel convention on the control of transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal.

I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave to the hon. Member for Stoke-on-Trent, North (Ms. Walley) on 27 October 1992, Official Report, column 534 and the answer my right hon. and learned Friend the Secretary of State for the Environment gave my hon. Friend the Member for Bromsgrove (Mr. Thomason) on 17 December, Official Report, column 506.

section.title: Energy Efficiency
section.p: Mr. Llew Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will publish a detailed breakdown of the increase from 1991–92 to 1992–93 for the energy efficiency office as listed at figures 8 and 20 of his Department's annual report 1993, Cm. 2207; and if he will make a statement on the effects upon the office of transfer to his Department.

Mr. Maclean: A breakdown of expenditure by the Energy Efficiency Office by programme area is given in figure 20 of the Department's annual report. This lists annual expenditure and future plans for the period 1987–88 to 1995–96.

The Government remain fully committed to the work of the EEO, which was transferred to the Department of the Environment in view of the environmental importance of energy efficiency. The EEO continues to offer and develop a wide range of programmes designed to encourage cost-effective improvements in energy efficiency in industry, commerce and the public sector and in the home.

section.title: Planning, South-East
section.p: Mr. Henderson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment when the draft regional planning guidance for the south-east will be published.
Mr. Baldry: My Department expects to publish new draft regional planning guidance for the south-east shortly.

Mr. Henderson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what plans his Department has to publish draft planning guidance for regions of the United Kingdom other than the south-east; and what account these will take of the plans for the south-east.

Mr. Baldry: Regional planning guidance was published for East Anglia in July 1991. Draft regional planning
301 guidance for the northern region was issued for consultation on 10 February 1993. Regional planning guidance will be issued for all other English regions by the end of 1993 or as early as possible thereafter. All regional planning guidance will take account of planning policies in other regions. Planning policies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are the responsibility of the respective Secretaries of State.

section.title: Business Rate
section.p: Mr. Henderson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what is his Department's estimate of the extent of the practice whereby buildings and property are stripped to avoid liability under the uniform business rate.

Mr. Robin Squire: We know of some cases where preliminary refurbishment or redevelopment work may have been brought forward to avoid rates. However, we are not aware of any empty properties that have been made unusable simply in order to avoid them.

section.title: West End Scheme, Bradford
section.p: Mr. Cryer: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what is the current position regarding the application by 3Ds Ltd. for city grant for the west end scheme in Bradford.

Mr. Robin Squire: An application has been made in respect of a first phase of the project. The appraisal was completed in November, but no decision has been taken because the applicants have yet to confirm whether they wish to proceed with the project.

section.p: Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what has been the total allocation, for each region, to home improvement agencies in England in 1991–92 and 1992–93.

In addition, we have allocated £290,000 in 1991–92 and £361,995 in 1992–93 to Care and Repair Ltd. as the national co-ordinating body for HIAs with responsibility for monitoring performance, providing training and specialist advice to agencies and undertaking scheme development.

section.title: Urban Partnership Fund
section.p: Mr. Anthony Coombs: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment which local authorities will receive assistance from the urban partnership fund; and if he will make a statement on the progress of the capital partnership programme.

Mr. Robin Squire [pursuant to the reply, 12 February 1993, c.834–25.]: An amended list of proposed projects for which we have offered support from the urban partnership fund has been placed in the Library today.

section.title: Capital Receipts
section.p: Mr. Straw: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will place in the Library on disk, and publish as soon as possible, a table showing for each local authority (a) its original estimate of capital receipts in 1992–93 and (b) its revised estimate capital receipts in 1992–93 recently supplied to his Department.

Mr. Howard: I have today placed in the Library a table showing the estimates of capital receipts in 1992–93 provided by each local authority on each of the three statistical returns received so far. All the estimates were
303 made before the relaxation in the rules governing the use of capital receipts by local authorities which was announced by my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer in his autumn statement.

section.title: Credit Liabilities
section.p: Mr. Straw: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment if he will place in the Library on disk, and publish as soon as it is available, a table showing for each local authority and for each region the amount set aside by local authorities as provision for credit liabilities at 31 March 1992.
Mr. Howard: Yes, when the full set of data from authorities is available. In previous years this has been about 15 months after the date to which the information relates.

section.title: Police Areas (Populations)
section.p: Mr. Sweeney: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment what was the resident population of each police force area in England in 1981 and 1991; and what was the day-time working population for the City of London police force area in 1981 and 1991.
Mr. Sackville: I have been asked to reply.

Estimated resident populations of the police force areas in England in 1981 and 1991 are shown in the table. The day-time working population of the City of London was about 300,000 in 1981. The results from the 1991 census of population, which are required to provide a corresponding figure for that year, are expected later this year.

section.title: Security Service
section.p: Mr. Winnick: To ask the right hon. Member for Berwick-upon-Tweed, representing the House of Commons Commission, what inquiries are made from the security services before appointments are made at Officer level in the House.

Mr. Beith: The security clearance procedures which apply to all staff of the House of Commons, whether Officers of the House or not, are directly analogous to those which apply to public servants. These were described in detail by the then Prime Minister on 24 July 1990 at columns 159–61.
Mr. Winnick: To ask the Lord President of the Council how many Adjournment debates on aspects of the security service took place in the Parliaments beginning in 1983 and 1987.
Mr. Newton: Three: on 4 April 1985, 3 December 1986 and 23 November 1988.
